title: Uranium Markets: Pricing, Supply, and the Fuel Cycle

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Nick, I've been following uranium for a while, and I have to say — what's happened in the last year feels different. Not just incremental progress, but a qualitative shift. Am I reading that right?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: You are. And I think the reason it feels different is that we've crossed the threshold from 'interesting science' to 'practical technology.' That's a transition that many fields never make. The fact that we're talking about pricing, supply, and the fuel cycle in terms of deployment timelines and unit economics, not just research papers — that's the signal.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Welcome to TechNova. I'm Dr. Sarah Chen.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: And I'm Marcus Webb. Today we're joined by Nick Touran, Nuclear Engineer at FastNeutron. Nick, welcome to the show.

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: Thanks for having me. Looking forward to this.

script.segment: SEGMENT 1: The State of the Field

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Nick, for listeners who are new to this topic, can you explain what uranium actually involves and why it matters?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: At its core, uranium is about SMR economics. That sounds simple, but the implications are profound. When you can do regulatory licensing reliably and at scale, it changes what's possible in Nuclear. The applications range from fuel cycle to construction timelines, and we're just scratching the surface.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: How did we get here? What was the path from idea to reality?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: It was a long path — decades, in some cases. The foundational research in government policy goes back years, but it was always limited by competing technologies. What changed is that we solved that limitation — through a combination of better technology, better understanding, and honestly, better computing power. Once the bottleneck cleared, everything downstream accelerated.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: And where are we now on that path?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: We're in the early deployment phase. The technology works. We're proving it in real-world conditions. The next challenge is scaling — making it cheaper, more reliable, and more accessible. That's an engineering challenge, not a science challenge, and engineering challenges are solvable with enough time and resources.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Nick, I want to get into the technical details. What makes your approach different from what's been tried before?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: The traditional approach to uranium relied on data center demand. It worked, but it had fundamental limitations — specifically, it didn't scale past a certain point. Our approach is different because we use international buildout to bypass those limitations entirely. Instead of trying to optimize within the old framework, we created a new framework.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What was the key insight that enabled that?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: It was actually a cross-disciplinary insight. Someone on our team had experience in fuel cycle, and they noticed a parallel between a problem in that field and our problem in uranium. They brought a technique over, adapted it, and it worked. The biggest breakthroughs often come from the intersection of fields, not from deep within one field.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: What's the current performance level, and what's the theoretical limit?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: We're currently at about 60 percent of what we believe is the theoretical limit. That might sound like there's a lot of headroom, but getting from 60 to 90 percent is often harder than getting from zero to 60. The last 10 percent — going from 90 to 100 — that's where you spend most of the effort. But even at 60 percent, we're already at a level where the technology is commercially viable.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Let's talk about impact. Who benefits from this, and how?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: The impact is broad. In the near term, investment landscape is the primary application — and that alone justifies the investment. But the second-order effects are where it gets really interesting. Once you have uranium working at scale, it enables things that weren't possible before — safety and public perception, new business models, new capabilities. It's a platform technology, not just a point solution.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: What about the risks? What could go wrong?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: I take risks seriously, and there are real ones. SMR economics at scale is untested — we're confident, but there could be surprises. There's the regulatory risk — if policymakers move too slowly, deployment stalls. And there's the societal risk — any transformative technology has distributional effects, and we need to be thoughtful about who benefits and who's displaced.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: How do you think about the ethical dimensions?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: It's something we discuss internally a lot. The technology itself is neutral — it's a tool. But how it's deployed, who has access to it, what safeguards are in place — those are choices, and they matter. I think the tech industry as a whole needs to do a better job of engaging with these questions proactively, not reactively.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Nick, what's your vision for where this field is in five years?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: In five years, I think uranium will be unremarkable — and that's the goal. When a technology becomes unremarkable, it means it's become infrastructure. It's just part of how things work. That's what happened with the internet, with smartphones, with cloud computing. I think uranium is on that same trajectory, and the five-year mark is when it crosses from 'exciting new technology' to 'standard tool that everyone uses.'

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What's the one thing you want our listeners to remember from this conversation?

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: That the future is being built right now, by people who are solving hard problems in labs and offices and factories. It's not science fiction — it's engineering. And engineering, when done well, is the most powerful force for progress that humanity has ever developed.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Nick Touran, Nuclear Engineer at FastNeutron. Thank you for a really thought-provoking conversation.

lines.speaker: Nick Touran
lines.text: Thank you both. I loved this.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: And thanks to all of you for listening. This is TechNova — see you next time.
